name: Osso Buco alla Milanese
historicNote: "Osso buco" literally means "bone with a hole", after the marrow-filled cross-cut veal shank the dish is built around. It emerged in 19th-century Milan, in Lombardy, where the original recipe (in bianco) used no tomato at all - just wine, broth, and vegetables - finished with gremolata, a raw mix of lemon zest, garlic, and parsley stirred in just before serving to cut through the richness.
whenEaten: A Sunday and holiday main course across Lombardy, traditionally paired with risotto alla Milanese so the saffron risotto can be eaten alongside the marrow spooned straight from the bone.
shortDescription: Cross-cut veal shanks braised low and slow until the meat falls from the bone, finished with a bright lemon-garlic-parsley gremolata.
headnote: The one thing worth being strict about is the cut itself: ask for cross-cut veal shank (osso buco cut), each piece tied around the middle with kitchen string so the marrow stays put while it braises. Everything else - the braising liquid, the vegetables underneath - is genuinely forgiving.
equipment: Wide, heavy-bottomed braising pan or dutch oven with a lid
Kitchen string to tie each shank
Fine grater or zester for the gremolata
miseEnPlace: Tie each veal shank around its middle with kitchen string before searing
Finely dice the onion, carrot, and celery (the soffritto) before starting
Zest the lemon just before making the gremolata so the oils stay fragrant

steps.title: Sear the shanks
steps.instruction: Dust {0001} in {0002} and shake off the excess, then brown well on both sides in {0003}. Set the shanks aside.

heat.flameNote: hot enough to brown quickly without burning the butter

steps.technique: Dry-dusting before searing builds a fond that thickens the braise later
steps.visualCue: Both cut faces are deep golden-brown, not grey
steps.commonMistake: Crowding the pan steams the meat instead of browning it - sear in batches if needed

steps.title: Build the soffritto and deglaze
steps.instruction: In the same pan, soften {0004}, {0005}, and {0006} in the rendered fat. Pour in {0007} and scrape up the browned bits from the bottom.

heat.flameNote: steady heat, not so high the wine reduces before the fond dissolves

steps.technique: Deglazing lifts the fond into the braising liquid instead of leaving it stuck to the pan
steps.visualCue: The wine has reduced by about half and the pan bottom is clean of stuck bits
steps.commonMistake: Skipping the deglaze loses most of the flavour the searing step built

steps.title: Braise low and slow
steps.instruction: Return the shanks to the pan standing upright so the marrow stays in the bone, add {0008} and {0009} until the liquid comes about two-thirds up the sides, cover, and braise.

heat.flameNote: a bare simmer, lid on, on the stovetop or in a 160C oven

steps.technique: Long, gentle braise breaks down the connective tissue without drying out the lean muscle
steps.visualCue: The meat has pulled back slightly from the bone and yields to a fork with no resistance
steps.commonMistake: Letting the braise boil rather than simmer toughens the meat instead of tenderizing it

steps.title: Finish with gremolata
steps.instruction: Combine {0010}, {0011}, and {0012}. Remove the string from the shanks and scatter the gremolata over the top just before serving.
steps.technique: Gremolata is added raw at the very end so its citrus and garlic stay bright against the rich braise
steps.visualCue: The gremolata sits visibly on top, not stirred into the sauce
steps.commonMistake: Adding the gremolata too early lets the heat dull its flavour

chefTips: Tying the shanks keeps the marrow from falling out mid-braise - always remove the string before plating
Make the braise a day ahead if possible; it reheats gently and tastes even better once the flavours settle
donenessSummary: The meat separates from the bone with light pressure from a fork, and the marrow is soft enough to scoop straight out.
platingNote: Serve one shank per person standing in a shallow pool of its own braising liquid, gremolata scattered on top, alongside risotto alla Milanese or soft polenta.
storageNote: Refrigerate up to 3 days in its braising liquid; reheat gently on the stovetop so the meat doesn't dry out.

substitutions.impact: Deeper, beefier flavour; needs roughly 30 extra minutes of braising

regionalVariations: A tomato-based version (in umido) is common outside Milan and in modern trattorias, though the original Milanese recipe is tomato-free
